title: Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
gist: Pangram, a 24-employee Brooklyn AI-detection startup that has raised $13 million, has become the de facto arbiter of AI authorship in publishing — killing book deals, integrating into Substack, and being used by literary agencies — despite documented weaknesses against humanizer tools, short text, and possible demographic bias.

themes.theme: A tiny company with outsized market power

insights.claim: Pangram has 24 employees and has raised $13 million total — about 0.0072 percent of what OpenAI has raised — yet functions as the arbiter of authorship for major publishing decisions.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The AI-verification layer is a capital-light, high-leverage niche adjacent to the frontier-model capex race — a category where small teams can capture disproportionate influence.
insights.quote: It has raised $13 million to date—about 0.0072 percent of what OpenAI has—and was virtually unknown until earlier this year.
insights.locator: Pangram is an AI startup with 24 employees

insights.claim: Pangram raised $9 million in July alongside launching Pangram 4, and has six open roles that would grow headcount 25 percent — a hiring pace signaling the company is scaling into demand rather than searching for it.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Most of the company's lifetime capital arrived in a single recent round, so the valuation reset for AI-detection happened in mid-2026 — a datable inflection for the subsector.
insights.locator: In July, Pangram raised $9 million

insights.claim: At least a dozen companies crowded the detection space by the time Pangram launched — including Originality.ai, GPTZero, and Turnitin — and Pangram broke out by performing well in early independent testing.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: In a commoditized category, third-party benchmark wins are the distribution mechanism — a fragile moat that a rival benchmark result can erase.
insights.locator: By then, at least a dozen other companies

insights.claim: Pangram's ambition is to be the go-to arbiter of originality for every sector — publishers, schools, and everyone else — with current customers spanning education, legal, and recruitment.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A horizontal verification layer across hiring, legal, and education is a far larger TAM than publishing alone — watch enterprise contracts, not literary scandals, for the real revenue story.
insights.quote: As far as I can tell, Pangram ultimately wants to be the go-to arbiter of originality for every sector: publishers, schools, and everyone else.
insights.locator: For now, Spero’s small team includes

insights.claim: Substack integrated Pangram into its platform in late July so readers can check possible AI use, positioning itself as neutral on AI while making disclosure a platform feature.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Platform-level integration is how detection becomes infrastructure rather than a tool — and Substack declining to disclose whether it pays per scan leaves the unit economics opaque.
insights.quote: Substack’s philosophy is not anti-AI. We simply believe you should know what you’re consuming.
insights.locator: We move on to Pangram’s Substack integration

insights.claim: Pangram scores have preceded the collapse of book deals: the self-published novel Shy Girl was scored 78 percent AI-generated by Pangram's CEO on X and Hachette later canceled its release.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A single unverified public score can void a publishing contract, which is real economic power held by a private vendor with no accountability mechanism.
insights.locator: In January, speculation swirled on Reddit

insights.claim: Public Pangram scores have hit a New York Times Modern Love column at 100 percent, a Commonwealth Short Story Prize winner at 100 percent, the novel Daggermouth at 60 percent, and a thriller that sold for $2.4 million at 97 percent.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Scores are being applied retroactively to prize winners and completed deals, creating open-ended contingent liability across publishers' existing catalogs.
insights.locator: A barrage of similar accusations followed

insights.claim: The CEO downplays Pangram's role in canceled book deals, saying the score is only a small part of a bigger picture — a framing that conveniently distances the company from the consequences of its own public accusations.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Liability-minimizing rhetoric from the vendor is worth noting given hints of brewing defamation suits from accused authors.
insights.quote: Basically, with every book deal, to my knowledge, it hasn’t really been about the Pangram score.
insights.locator: Pangram hasn’t exactly shied away from controversy

insights.claim: The Shy Girl manuscript that Pangram's CEO scored and posted publicly came from a pirating website, and he acknowledged he had not looked closely at its provenance before running it.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A trust-and-verification vendor sourcing evidence from a piracy site undercuts the credibility its entire business model depends on.
insights.quote: Yeah. And, like, yeah … it is what it is. I hadn’t looked too closely.
insights.locator: Another twist: Critics of Pangram

insights.claim: The public narrative that Pangram was merely a passive tool in the Shy Girl story is wrong: a Pangram account executive discussed the story with a publishing industry analyst who then brought it to The New York Times.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Sales staff seeding scandals to press is a growth strategy, not incidental — it means reputational blowback risk scales with revenue.
insights.quote: Like a game of AI-scandal telephone, it was a Pangram account executive who discussed the story with a publishing industry analyst who, in turn, brought it to the Times.
insights.locator: Except that wasn’t exactly how it happened

insights.claim: Pangram employed a contractor who described himself as an 'attack dog', consulting on social strategy while publicly calling out suspected AI users, before the company parted ways with him.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The company's early growth ran on public shaming; the pivot away from it is the clearest evidence management sees that channel as a liability.
insights.quote: I wanted to take a harsher approach because I thought that people were getting off too easy
insights.locator: According to Rod Breslau, a journalist

insights.claim: A Notre Dame working paper found Pangram's 3.2 model flagged light AI editing of academic abstracts as AI writing 64 to 80 percent of the time, but caught AI-generated text run through a humanizer less than 4 percent of the time.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A sub-4 percent catch rate against a trivially available countermeasure means the detection layer is defeated by a cheap adversarial tool — the core technical risk to the whole category.
insights.quote: after putting AI-generated text through a humanizer—a tool that makes AI work seem more human—Pangram caught AI writing less than 4 percent of the time.
insights.locator: A new working paper from Notre Dame

insights.claim: Pangram claims a false positive rate of 0.0041 percent with its new model, improved from a previously reported 0.01 percent, achieved partly by deliberately erring toward declaring borderline text human-written.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The headline accuracy number is purchased with false negatives — the metric optimizes for defensibility against lawsuits rather than for actually catching AI text.
insights.quote: This is an intentional choice that we made
insights.locator: All told, Pangram claims false positives

insights.claim: By Pangram's own measure, human essays heavily rewritten by AI are still classified as human-written 41.37 percent of the time.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A miss rate above 40 percent on heavy AI rewriting means the tool cannot support the enforcement decisions publishers and schools are already making with it.
insights.quote: human essays that are heavily rewritten by AI are still detected as human-written 41.37 percent of the time.
insights.locator: By Pangram’s measure

insights.claim: Pangram performs worse on text under 100 words while its median input is 350 words and its free tier caps at roughly 2,000 words a day, and the company concedes an identical passage can get different verdicts depending on whether it is scanned alone or in larger context.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Context-dependent, non-reproducible verdicts are disqualifying for any evidentiary use — a direct exposure point in the defamation suits the article says may be brewing.
insights.locator: Pangram does disclose that its tool performs worse

insights.claim: Writers have already learned to game the system by tweaking text or writing deliberately like AI to elicit false results, according to a researcher who works closely with the company.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Two-sided gaming — evading detection and inducing false accusations — makes detection an unstable arms race rather than a solved verification problem.
insights.quote: Of course, you can fool Pangram
insights.locator: “Of course, you can fool Pangram,”

insights.claim: Pangram trains by 'synthetic mirroring' — having LLMs generate close matches to human writing — plus 'hard negative mining' that hunts datasets for false positives to retrain against, and its datasets are licensed partly because the product is far less data-hungry than frontier models.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Clean licensed data is a genuine differentiator for a company selling trust — and is only affordable because detection needs orders of magnitude less data than generation.
insights.quote: All of our datasets are properly licensed, which I think is kind of rare in the AI world today
insights.locator: To detect AI, Pangram uses a method

insights.claim: A professor of critical AI literacy argues detectors do not work and are prejudiced against certain people, citing a study showing detectors more often flag non-native English writers, with neurodiverse writers reporting the same.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Disparate-impact claims are the most likely regulatory attack surface for detection vendors in education and hiring, where anti-discrimination law already applies.
insights.quote: I don’t think [AI detectors] work. I think that detectors are prejudiced against certain people.
insights.locator: Critics point to two major issues with Pangram

insights.claim: The three biggest AI-detection scandals in publishing — Shy Girl, Daggermouth, and Call Me, I'll Hide the Body — were all written by writers of color, and whose work gets scanned is itself a human, bias-prone decision.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Selection bias in who gets tested is a discrimination risk independent of model accuracy — and it is the head of a major agent association raising it.
insights.quote: As an African American agent, I do think we really need to pay attention to some of the inequities within the industry
insights.locator: The three novels mentioned earlier

insights.claim: The academic whose 14,419-novel study became the most-cited evidence for AI in self-publishing receives free API credits from Pangram, calls the CEO a close friend, publicly defends the company, and is in a relationship with a literary agency co-CEO who both uses and consults for Pangram.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The independent validation underpinning the company's credibility is entangled with the company itself — a disclosed conflict that weakens the strongest external evidence for the product.
insights.locator: I wanted Chakrabarty’s perspective

insights.claim: The same researcher's Pangram-based analysis of 14,419 self-published novels found nearly 20 percent had substantial AI-detection scores, and that data was the original source for the Daggermouth accusations.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: A 20 percent AI-involvement estimate in self-publishing is the number that will anchor policy debates — even though it is generated by the tool whose accuracy is in question.
insights.locator: When Tuhin Chakrabarty, an assistant professor

insights.claim: Pangram's CEO has offered cash bounties to writers who claim wrongful flagging and can prove they wrote the work themselves, saying he offers it where he is almost certain the person is lying, and that nobody has claimed it so far.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: An unclaimed bounty is being used as a credibility proxy, but the selection criterion — only offering it where he already believes the writer is lying — makes it evidentially worthless.
insights.quote: I’ve offered the bounty in cases where I’m almost certain the person is lying
insights.locator: In some cases where writers have claimed

insights.claim: A Gotham Ghostwriters poll of 1,481 working writers found 61 percent use AI tools and 7 percent have published AI-generated text, establishing that AI use in writing is already majority behavior rather than a fringe practice.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: If 61 percent of professional writers already use AI, detection cannot function as a binary gate — the industry will be forced toward disclosure norms instead of prohibition.
insights.locator: Still, the reality is that AI is used

insights.claim: Of the Big Five publishers, only Penguin Random House confirmed editors may use approved AI-detection tools, stressing they are not determinative; Simon & Schuster and HarperCollins declined comment and Hachette and Macmillan did not respond.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Publisher silence signals adoption without disclosure — the enterprise revenue is likely larger than public statements suggest, and so is the litigation exposure.
insights.locator: I reached out to the Big Five publishers

insights.claim: A top New York literary agency began using Pangram on manuscripts and proposals and immediately had to confront authors whose works scored between 50 and 95 percent AI-written, with some asked to rewrite in their own voice.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Agencies are the real chokepoint — deals are being killed offstage before publishers ever see them, so public scandals undercount the market impact.
insights.quote: Right away, we started having to have difficult conversations [with authors] because Pangram was showing their works to be anything from 50 percent AI written to 95 percent.
insights.locator: Chakrabarty encouraged Shuster to meet with Pangram

insights.claim: Writers direct as much or more hostility at detection software as at the AI companies themselves, per an author and publishing expert quoted in the piece.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The customer base's own creators are the vendor's loudest opponents — a brand risk that constrains how far detection can be pushed into consumer-facing products.
insights.quote: There’s this feeling like they are just as evil, if not more evil, than the AI companies themselves.
insights.locator: Not all writers see this as a good thing

insights.claim: Pangram has changed strategy on the expectation that AI use will become more accepted, pivoting from chasing all AI users to flagging deception and building higher-granularity detection that identifies even light AI editing.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: The vendor itself is betting the prohibition market shrinks and the disclosure-and-granularity market grows — a strategic read worth adopting for the whole detection sector.
insights.quote: Higher granularity, better detail, provide more information to the end users.
insights.locator: Pangram parted ways with Breslau

insights.claim: Pangram's stated competitive strategy is transparency — publishing technical reports on its models and training — explicitly contrasted against rivals it characterizes as black boxes.
insights.speaker: Lexi Pandell
insights.so_what: Transparency is the only available moat in a commoditized category, but publishing model details also hands humanizer developers a roadmap to defeat it.
insights.quote: Everybody else is sort of this black box, so I think our strategy here is really just build trust through transparency
insights.locator: He plans to continue publishing technical reports
